goal: Pick one task from your current job or the job you want. You'll run it through three assistants today.

steps.label: Write your goal
steps.why: Every lab starts with your own task so the work matters to you.
do: Think of one task you do (or will do) regularly: a weekly report, answering customer emails, planning a schedule.
Type it in one or two sentences in the box below. Be specific: 'Summarize my team's weekly sales numbers into a short update' beats 'reporting'.
steps.see: A one or two sentence goal in the box. That's it.

checkpoint.prompt: Your task, in one or two sentences
checkpoint.placeholder: Example: Draft replies to the five most common customer questions at my store.

steps.label: Create your three accounts
steps.why: You'll compare the three big assistants side by side all course long.
do: Open chatgpt.com and click Sign up. Use your Google account to skip a password.
Open claude.ai and do the same.
Open gemini.google.com. It signs in with the same Google account automatically.
Leave all three tabs open.
steps.see: Three browser tabs, each with an empty chat box and a blinking cursor.
steps.tip: If a site asks for a phone number, that's normal for the free tier. If you'd rather not, ask your instructor for the class backup account.

checkpoint.prompt: All three tabs are open and I can type in each one.

steps.label: Write three questions
steps.why: Writing questions before you ask stops the assistant from steering you.
do: Open a new Google Doc and title it 'Week 1 Day 1 comparison'.
Write three questions about your task that you'd ask an experienced coworker. One factual (what is...), one how-to (how would I...), one judgment (should I...).
Number them 1, 2, 3.
steps.see: A doc with your goal at the top and three numbered questions.

steps.label: Ask all three assistants
steps.why: Same question, three answers. The differences are the lesson.
do: Copy question 1. Paste it into ChatGPT, press Enter. Paste the same text into Claude and Gemini.
Under question 1 in your doc, paste each answer with a label: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini.
Repeat for questions 2 and 3.
steps.see: Nine answers in your doc, three under each question. Some will be long; that's fine.
steps.tip: If an assistant asks you a clarifying question instead of answering, type 'Just give me your best answer' and continue.

checkpoint.prompt: Quick check: the three assistants gave different answers to the same question. Why?
options: They predict likely text from different training and settings, so there's no single 'correct' output
checkpoint.why: Each assistant predicts the next words from its own training and settings. Different models, different predictions. None of them looked anything up unless you saw a 'searching' indicator.

steps.label: Mark what's wrong or vague
steps.why: Spotting the weak spots is the skill. Trusting output blindly is the trap.
do: Read each answer. Highlight in yellow anything that's wrong, made up, or so vague it doesn't help.
If an answer looks perfect, reply to the assistant: 'What's your source for that?' and highlight anything it can't back up.
Aim for at least one highlight per assistant.
steps.see: Yellow highlights across your doc. At least three total.

checkpoint.prompt: Describe the worst mistake you found and which assistant made it
checkpoint.placeholder: Example: Gemini said my state's sales tax is 4% but it's 8%.

steps.label: Sort eight real applications
steps.why: This is Domain 1 of the exam: knowing which kind of problem is which.
do: Decide whether each is Regression (predicts a number), Classification (picks a category), or Clustering (finds groups without labels):
Fraud detection · Sales forecasting · Movie recommendations · Spam filter · House price prediction · Grouping customers by behavior · Photo tagging · Demand planning
Write your eight answers, one per line, with a short reason.
steps.see: Eight lines. Typical answers: fraud = classification, forecasting = regression, recommendations = clustering or classification, spam = classification, house price = regression, customer groups = clustering, photo tagging = classification, demand = regression.

checkpoint.prompt: Grouping customers by shopping behavior, with no labels given, is:
checkpoint.why: No labels and the goal is to find natural groups: that's clustering. Classification needs labeled categories to learn from.

steps.label: Upload your doc
do: Take a screenshot of your comparison doc showing at least one highlighted answer, or set the doc to 'Anyone with the link can view' and copy the link.
Upload it below.
steps.see: A thumbnail of your screenshot, or your link, in the submissions list.

checkpoint.prompt: Screenshot or link to your comparison doc

stretch: Ask each assistant to describe its own limits, then fact-check one claim it made about itself using an official source
Rewrite your weakest question so all three assistants give a useful answer
doneWhen: Three assistants, nine answers, at least three highlights
All eight applications sorted with one reason each

submission.prompt: Upload a screenshot of your comparison doc, or paste a link to it.

lens.plain: A model plus tools plus a loop that decides its next step.
lens.exam: Domain 1: agentic AI as the newest layer of AI.

lens.plain: AI that creates new content instead of only predicting a label.
lens.exam: Domain 1: generative AI built on deep learning.

lens.plain: You need an exact repeatable answer, there's not enough good data, or the cost outweighs the value.
lens.exam: Domain 1: when AI/ML is and isn't appropriate.

lens.plain: Sorting into categories vs predicting a number.
lens.exam: Domain 1: real-world use cases by problem type.

quiz.q: Which statement about the AI family tree is correct?
a: Machine learning is a type of generative AI
Deep learning sits inside machine learning, which sits inside AI
Generative AI replaced machine learning in 2022
AI and machine learning are the same thing
quiz.why: AI is the umbrella. Machine learning is inside it, deep learning inside that, and generative AI is built on deep learning.

quiz.q: A pharmacy needs the exact same tax calculation every time. Why is AI the wrong tool?
a: AI is too expensive for pharmacies
AI gives plausible answers, not guaranteed exact ones
AI can't do math at all
quiz.why: When you need an exact, repeatable answer every time, a rule or formula beats a model that predicts.

quiz.q: Predicting next month's sales figure is an example of:
quiz.why: Regression predicts a number. Classification sorts into categories. Clustering finds groups.

quiz.q: What makes an AI system an agent rather than a chatbot?
a: It can take actions with tools and decide its next step
quiz.why: An agent is a model plus tools plus a loop that decides what to do next.

quiz.q: Which was the 2017 breakthrough that today's language models build on?
quiz.why: The 2017 transformer paper introduced attention, the mechanism inside every modern LLM.
